overview: This four-document file concerns Japanese controls over navigation and maritime movement in and around Japan and Japanese-occupied Shanghai during 1941. Three cross-reference sheets point to records filed elsewhere: a protest over refusal to let American President Lines vessels pass the Nantao boom at Shanghai, restrictions preventing foreigners and American missionaries from traveling on the Seto Inland Sea, and requested statistics on merchant ships entering and clearing Vladivostok. The sole full telegram reports a Hōchi columnist’s call for Japan to close the Tsugaru and Soya straits in retaliation for the exclusion of Japanese shipping from the Panama Canal and to stop strategic supplies bound for Vladivostok.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on President Lines vessels and the Nantao boom
subfiles.from: Frank P. Lockhart, Shanghai (sender of referenced telegram)
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to Shanghai telegram no. 678 concerning Japanese refusal to permit American President Lines vessels to pass the Nantao boom.
subfiles.summary: The matter was raised with the Japanese Consulate General, but the resulting understanding was that the Japanese had no intention of permitting the requested passage. The refusal was characterized as a complete disregard of American rights and interests. The original telegram was filed under decimal number 793.94.

subfiles.title: Grew telegram on proposals to close the Tsugaru and Soya straits
subfiles.about: Grew reports a Hōchi column advocating closure of Japan’s northern straits to ships of hostile powers.
subfiles.summary: Columnist Emoto argued that Japan should close the Tsugaru and Soya straits because the United States had closed the Panama Canal to Japanese ships. He maintained that vessels belonging to nations hostile to Japan should not be allowed through Japanese waters. The article also warned that munitions, aircraft, and high-test gasoline were being shipped to Vladivostok and stressed the growing defensive importance of Hokkaido and Karafuto.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on restrictions on foreign travel in the Seto Inland Sea
subfiles.from: Sobokin, Kobe (as rendered in the text; sender of referenced telegram)
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a Kobe telegram reporting a temporary prohibition on foreign travel in the Seto Inland Sea.
subfiles.summary: Japanese navigation regulations prohibited all foreigners from traveling on the Seto Inland Sea between February 15 and 25. American missionaries were consequently prevented from traveling by steamer. The original record was filed under decimal number 894.81/14.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on merchant ships entering and clearing Vladivostok
subfiles.from: Angus I. Ward, Vladivostok (apparent sender of referenced telegram)
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to Vladivostok telegram no. 61 supplying requested details about merchant-ship arrivals and departures.
subfiles.summary: The referenced telegram furnished the names and nationalities of merchant vessels entering and clearing port. It also supplied their flags, arrival and departure dates, last ports of call, and destinations. The original telegram was filed under decimal number 861.8591/15.

interest: The file brings together several distinct dimensions of maritime control immediately before the Pacific War: restrictions imposed on American commercial shipping in occupied Shanghai, controls on foreigners traveling within Japan, public advocacy for closing strategic straits, and systematic observation of Soviet-port traffic. Grew’s telegram is especially useful for studying how Japanese commentators framed restrictions on navigation as retaliation for U.S. policy and connected them to strategic shipments to Vladivostok. The cross-reference sheets also reveal how relevant evidence was dispersed across the State Department’s decimal filing system, including a February document predating the nominal June–September span of the file.
